title: Kopan
text:
Kopan Street is a Korean style Hotteok Bar located in the beautiful city of Copenhagen, Denmark. A staple of Korean street food in the city since 2014, they specialize in hotteok a common South Korean street food consisting of a pan-fried pastry of sweet yeasted dough and filled with varies foods ranging from sweet melted brown sugar and nuts to savory bulgogi and kimchi. As the first and only Hotteok bar in Europe, there were big expectations going into this meal.


As this is a street bar, the venue was quiet small but has an amazing contemporary style that was not afraid to use color and various tiles. There was a welcoming environment as soon as you entered, with polite employees and a small photobooth where customers are allowed to take photos while waiting for their food.
During my visit, I tried the kimchi bulgogi hotteok with sriracha and sesame seeds. A simple finger food styled meal based on traditional Korean staples.










Kopan Kimchi Bulgogi Hotteok





When I say this was the best Korean food I had in Copenhagen, you have to believe me. The warm sweet pastry mixed with the savory and tangy after notes of the bulgogi and kimchi were perfect for a rainy day. I have to rate Kopan Street 5 stars.
An easy meal if your in a quick bind, that can transition smoothly into an afternoon bite to have while chatting with a friend. I recommend this spot for all occasions if your in Copenhagen looking for a nice Korean treat.
After visiting this location while abroad, I took my friends a week later and took my entire family when they visited me a month after.

★★★★★

title: Mad & Kaffe
text:
Mad & Kaffe is a chain brunch restaurant located across Copenhagen, Denmark. With their name quite literally translating to Food & Coffee from Danish, they pride themselves on providing a local environment centered on a love for food and coffee while making it feel like you never left your Danish apartment.
They have four locations across the city, all providing the same menu. Their dining style resembles a “build your own breakfast” where you can choose a spread of 3, 5, of 7 items from their menu. Allowing for unlimited combinations to make the meal especially your own.


The restaurant itself was beautiful having a homely danish feel from their furniture to natural lighting. They create an atmosphere that encapsulates hygge with throw pillows and blankets at ever table.
While there I got a hot matcha, scrambled eggs, a spinach and feta quiche, and a small bowl of overnight oats.













Mad & Kaffe Menus











Matcha and Brunch








This was an delicious and light brunch that got me ready to tackle the rest of the day. The coffee and matcha were perfectly warm for a cold day and tasted perfect. The meal itself was a perfect variety of sweet from the overnight oats and savory from the fluffy scrambled eggs and the smooth quiche.
While on the more trendy site, these places on social media are popular for a reason. The novelty of picking your own items and the beautiful curated atmosphere make this place a must stop by when in the city. I ended up taking not only my parents but my best friend when she visited.
I would give Mad & Kaffe 5 stars!

★★★★★

Education
I currently am attending the University of California, Santa Barbara. I am pursing a Bachelor of Science in Environmental Studies with a concentration in Physical Geography. I have taken courses ranging from introductory sciences series like chemistry and physics to more defined upper division courses focused on renewable energy systems and GIS applications within the environmental field.

title: About Me!
text:
Career Opportunites and Goals
I currently am interning at the Santa Barbara County Association of Governments, aiding with technical GIS applications for our counties transportation routes and systems. My tasks range from constructing maps depictining demographics and transportations across Santa Barbara County, building web based applications used as guidance for county supervisor’s decisions, and conducting GIS governance for the organization’s data hub. It has been an amazing opprotunity to expand my familairty with Esri Suite and learn more about the intricasies associated transportation planning on a county wide level.
Additionally, I am a Sustainability Support Staff Lead at the Isla Vista Community Service District. I mainly support the districts compost opperations, doing hands on tasks like building piles and servicing drop off bins but I also schedule and conduct volunteer opportunites, oversee community outreach by tabling at certain events, and create operational material guides for future employees.
I also work for Associated Students Recycling on UCSB campus as a Route Rider. In this position, I help facilitate on campus recycling to meet UCSB’s sustainability goals. While it might not be the most glamorous job, I have loved connecting with fellow UCSB students over a shared passion of enhancing the universities commitment to environmental stewardship.
Finally, while not a paid position, I currently am acting as the Development Manager for Sprout Up UCSB. Sprout Up aims to provide free environmental science education to Title I elementary schools across the nation. We hope to foster not only a love for the environment but science in general by providing novel lessons and experiments that these schools might not have access to. As the Development Manager, I organize and oversee fundraising events like raffle baskets, resteraunt collaborations, and our annual 5k.

title: ENVS Statistics Midterm
text:
Below I have included my code and text from the third question of my Data Science midterm, where I explore and recreate an analysis of the difference in median Black Queen Cell Virus pathogen load of Bombus impatiens workers in valley, edge, and forest environments. I will first identify the variables, the test type, and hypotheses. Then I will clean the data and summarize a tabular display. Finally, I will run the associated statistical test and effectively communicate the findings.



The response variable is pathogen load, specifically Deformed Wing Virus, Black Queen Cell Virus, Vairimorpha bombi, and Crithidia bombi measured in Bombus impatiens worker. This variable would be continuous.
The predictor variable was the habitat type and the landscape variables. The groups for the habitat type were valley, edge, and forest, where as, the landscape variables ranged from non-forest natural, grassland/pasture, Developed open, Developed, Barren, Open water, crops, and to forest.
The response variables were measured by performing quantitative PCRs on pooled abdomens of three B. impatiens workers per sample and analyzing 1-3 pools per site. These measurements then gave clear data on pathogen load within the sample(Gratton, E., et al., 2023. “Local habitat type influences bumble bee pathogens loads and bee species distributions.” Environmental Entomology 52:3 May 2023, paragraph 10 of the paper, paragraph 3 of the methods section, or paragraph 1 of the pathogen quantification section).




The test that the researchers used was a Kruskal-Wallis test and then a Dunn post-hoc test (Gratton, E., et al., 2023. “Local habitat type influences bumble bee pathogens loads and bee species distributions.” Environmental Entomology 52:3 May 2023, paragraph 18 of the paper, paragraph 11 of the methods section, which is also paragraph 1 of the statistical analysis portion)



\(H_O\): There is no difference in the median BQCV pathogen load of Bombus impatiens worker in valleys, edges, and forests.
\(H_A\): There is a difference in the median BQCV pathogen load of Bombus impatiens worker in valleys, edges, and forests.





Code
#read in tidyverse
library(tidyverse)
# read in janitor
library(janitor)
# read in flextable
library(flextable)
# read in rstatix
library (rstatix)
# read in here package
library(here)
# read in data
bee_pathogens <- read_csv(here("Posts", "ENVS_Midterm", "bee-pathogens.csv"))




Code
#create object bee_pathogens_clean
bee_pathogens_clean <- bee_pathogens |>
  # clean names, making lower case and underscores
  clean_names() |>
  # remove na values
  drop_na() |>
  # keep only site type and BQCV columns
  select(site_type_x, bqcv) |>
  # rename site type to habitat
  rename(habitat = site_type_x)
#display 10 rows from bee_pathogens_clean
slice_sample(bee_pathogens_clean, n = 10, by = NULL, weight_by = NULL, 
             replace = FALSE)


# A tibble: 10 × 2
   habitat   bqcv
   <chr>    <dbl>
 1 forest  10.9  
 2 forest   9.39 
 3 forest   6.87 
 4 valley   8.42 
 5 forest   0    
 6 edge     9.07 
 7 edge     6.41 
 8 valley   4.02 
 9 forest   1.000
10 valley   8.62 







Code
# create object bee_pathogens_summary
bee_pathogens_summary <- bee_pathogens_clean |>
  # group by habitat type
  group_by(habitat) |>
  # start the summary for bee_pathogen_summary data
  summarize(
    #calculate the median BQCV load
    median_bqcv = round(median(bqcv), 1),
    # calculate the number of observations
    n = n())
# display summary calculations with flextable
flextable(bee_pathogens_summary) |>
  # remove underscore and capitalize
  set_header_labels(median_bqcv = "Median BQCV", habitat = "Habitat", 
                    n = "Sample Size") |>
  # autofit to fit titles on one line
  autofit()


HabitatMedian BQCVSample Sizeedge6.327forest5.024valley7.629







Code
# start kruskal-wallis test
kruskal.test(
  # formula: bqcv load as a function of habitat
  bqcv ~ habitat,
  # data: clean bee pathogen data frame
  data = bee_pathogens_clean
)



    Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test

data:  bqcv by habitat
Kruskal-Wallis chi-squared = 9.8219, df = 2, p-value = 0.007365







Code
# start Dunn's Post-Hoc Test
dunn_test(
  #formula: bqcv ratings as a function of habitat
  bqcv ~ habitat,
  # data: clean bee pathogen data frame
  data = bee_pathogens_clean
)


# A tibble: 3 × 9
  .y.   group1 group2    n1    n2 statistic       p   p.adj p.adj.signif
* <chr> <chr>  <chr>  <int> <int>     <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl> <chr>       
1 bqcv  edge   forest    27    24     -1.83 0.0679  0.136   ns          
2 bqcv  edge   valley    27    29      1.31 0.189   0.189   ns          
3 bqcv  forest valley    24    29      3.13 0.00175 0.00525 **          







Code
# start effect size calculation
kruskal_effsize(
  # formula: bqcv ratings as a function of habitat
  bqcv ~ habitat,
  # data: clean bee pathogen data frame
  data = bee_pathogens_clean
)


# A tibble: 1 × 5
  .y.       n effsize method  magnitude
* <chr> <int>   <dbl> <chr>   <ord>    
1 bqcv     80   0.102 eta2[H] moderate 





There was a moderate effect (\(\eta^2\) = 0.102) of habitat type on BQCV loads (Fig. 2a. Kruskal-Wallis, \(\chi^2\) = 9.82, df = 2, P = 0.007, \(\alpha\) = 0.05) with significant differences between the median values of valley (n = 29, \(\bar{x}\) = 7.6) and forest (n = 24, \(\bar{x}\) = 5.0, \(\chi^2\) = 9.82, Dunn’s Test, z = -3.13, P-adj = 0.005). While edge habitats had a greater median (n = 27, \(\bar{x}\) = 6.3, \(\chi^2\) = 9.82) than forest there was no difference found (Dunn’s Test, z = -1.83, P-adj = 0.236), and while edge habitat median was less than valley median, no difference was found (Dunn’s Test, z = 3.13, P-adj = 0.189)

title: Reenvisioning Recycling
text:
During my second year of undergrad, I participated in a 9 month program called the Environmental Leadership Incubator. This program provided student’s with the resources and support to undertake an environmental related passion project of their choosing.
Along with my project partner, Ella Graban, I focused on establishing a thin film recycling program for the Isla Vista and UCSB community. This plastic is commonly used within our society, seen as any form of bread bags, pallet wrap, and even some forms of plastic bags, however it is not conventionally recycled through modern waste facilities. This leads to large amounts of this plastic building up in our landfills, natural environment, and even our bodies.
Through a partnership with Planet Protectors, based out of Downtown Santa Barbara we were able to start collecting this plastic from local sources and even directly from the community through weekly pickups and donation drop-off locations. After collecting within our own community, we would deliver it to their location downtown where it would eventually be transported to be melted into smaller pellets and later turned into plastic decking and chairs through the company treks.
Below is an interactive map depicting the locations around UCSB and Isla Vista where we had weekly pickups and drop-off sites.


Code
# loading necessary library
library(sf) # spatial data handling
library(leaflet) # interactive map creation
library(htmltools) # HTML rendering for labels and popups
library(janitor) # cleaning columns
library(tidyverse) # data manipulation and piping
library(readr) # read csv with data
library(here) # locate files




Code
# load csv and clean columns
Plastic <- read_csv(here("Posts", "ELI", "ELI_Map.csv")) |>
            clean_names()

# set colors
pal <- colorFactor(
  palette = c("skyblue", "coral"),
  levels = c("Pick Up", "Drop Off"))

# build interactive map for ELI data
leaflet(data = Plastic) |>
  addProviderTiles("Esri.WorldImagery") |> # Satalitte background
  setView(lng = -119.846, lat = 34.413, zoom = 15) |> # set opening position 
  
  # interactive marker that show location in popup
  addCircleMarkers(~latitude,
             ~longitude,
             color = ~pal(type_of_location),
             fillColor = ~pal(type_of_location),
             fill = TRUE,
             radius = 8,
             fillOpacity = 1,
             stroke = FALSE,
             popup = ~paste(location, "<br>", type_of_location)) |>
  #add legend for colors
  addLegend(
    pal = pal,
    values = ~type_of_location,
    title = "Type of Location"
  )

title: Stephen Bond
text:
Welcome!
Hello, thanks for stopping by my website! My name is Stephen, a current third year Environmental Studies major with a concentration in Physical Geography at UCSB.
While I currently call Santa Barbara home, I am originally from Massachusetts.
This website acts as a collection of my academic and professional experiences, personal interests, and some delicious recipes. I hope this provides a little slice of who I am!


Currently
While I still am in undergad, I currently work for the Santa Barbara County Association of Governments as a GIS intern, the Isla Vista Community Service district as a Sustainability Staff Lead, and Associated Students Recycling as a route Rider. I learned from these positions that I find the my work most meaningful when it is rooted in local government and community initiatives. Seeing hard work overtime directly benefit a place so close to home is what drives me to continue making advancements to our community and bolster environmental initiatives.
When I am not too busy working, I love volunteering for Sprout Up a national nonprofit focused on providing free environmental education to Title I elementary schools. I also find myself enjoying a good board game with my friends and family, exploring the outdoors, or traveling.

title: DubuHaus
text:
When visiting my brother in New York City, I was fortunate enough to visit the lovely, DubuHaus in Koreatown, Midtown Manhattan. This restaurant specializes in traditional and contemporary Korean dished. They are especially know for their in house Dubu, made with organic, non-GMO soybeans daily.


The restaurant was beautifully furnished modern wooden pieces, simple and sleek dining ware, and back lit for a perfect dining experience.
During my visit, I enjoyed a sample of their fresh soy milk, delicious array of banchan, Korean Pancakes Platter (kimchi mushroom, leek, and zucchini with mungbean), and for my entree the Dubu Vegetable Bibimbap. The meal culminated in a delicious vanilla bean soft serve.













Dubu Vegetable Bibimbap











My Mother and I at DubuHaus








I would rate DubuHaus 5 stars! The selection of apetizers and entrees captured the love of Korean cuisine and with each bite you could tell care and effort was put into your food.
The waiters were exceptionally generous with banchan which is something I would never say no too!
If you are every in New York City, I definetly recommend adding this stop to your list.

★★★★★
